# shad0w

> shad0w (pip install shad0wllm, npm i shad0wllm) learns the fixed-choice decisions an application sends to an LLM
> (intents, routing, moderation, agent tool choice), and answers the ones it can certify from a small table on the CPU in
> microseconds. Every other request still goes to the LLM, and its answer is logged so the table keeps learning. The
> certificate (Learn-then-Test with Clopper-Pearson bounds) states that, among served answers, disagreement with the LLM
> is at most alpha (default 5%) with 90% confidence. It works in front of chat models, the OpenAI Decisions API and System
> One decision models (Jev, Kev, Laya), from Python, JavaScript, C or HTTP, or with zero code through an OpenAI-compatible
> proxy. Apache-2.0, by Gaurav Chauhan.

## Blog
- [Adding a category without breaking production](https://2796gaurav.github.io/shad0w/blog/adding-a-category.html): A trained shortcut and a changing list of options are a dangerous mix. What goes wrong, the rule shad0w follows now, and the lifecycle of an option from rename to retirement.
- [System Zero: the reflex layer your LLM stack is missing](https://2796gaurav.github.io/shad0w/blog/system-zero.html): LLMs think slowly. Decision models think fast. But most of what an app asks is a repeat, and repeats need a reflex. A case for System Zero, and how shad0w implements it.
- [How can a small table promise it agrees with your LLM?](https://2796gaurav.github.io/shad0w/blog/how-the-certificate-works.html): The certificate behind shad0w, in plain words: a held-out test, a confidence line, an allowance for bad luck, and what the promise does and does not cover.
- [What we measured: where shad0w wins, and where it loses](https://2796gaurav.github.io/shad0w/blog/what-we-measured.html): Real LLMs, real proxies, public datasets and the same certifier for every method. The numbers that make shad0w worth using, and the ones that show when not to.
